A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, retaining the mechanism, main robustness theorem and Facebook experiments. All pages, equations and figures were readable. Both documents end with references; neither contains an appendix.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original perturbation experiments on 120-node and 574-node Facebook graphs, using 100 random perturbations per probability.

after.justification: Section 5 retains original Facebook experiments and adds larger-noise results and average clustering distances in Figures 5.2 and 5.3.

M1.justification: Both versions apply randomized edge flipping followed by the same two-way spectral clustering procedure: compute the second Laplacian eigenvector, order vertices and minimize the cut ratio. Naming possible eigensolvers in v2 adds implementation guidance without establishing an algorithm change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Facebook clustering task and report graphs with 120 and 574 retained vertices. However, the second input filename changes from 1609.edges to 1684.edges without explaining whether this corrects identification or replaces data. The PDFs do not establish an actual dataset substitution; the larger probability sweeps otherwise extend the existing perturbation setting.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally compares against alternative clustering or privacy methods. Both compare spectral clustering on original and perturbed graphs. Added citations do not introduce evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The original probability grid, p = 0.0001q for q = 1 through 50, is retained. New sweeps in Figure 5.2 extend to approximately 0.25 and 0.05 for the respective graphs, while Figure 5.3 reports averages through 0.10. The original graph sizes, pruning rule and 100-trial design remain documented.

E4.justification: New Sections 5.1 and 5.2 investigate robustness at substantially larger perturbations and distinguish maximum from average clustering discrepancies. They add failure-case analysis involving alternative partitions of Facebook1684. Figure 1.1 also adds a before-and-after neighborhood example, extending the earlier small-noise verification substantially.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly identifies the low-noise curve as the maximum over 100 trials and adds mean-distance summaries over 100 iterations. This changes statistical summarization and clarifies aggregation, without documenting an increase in repetitions. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, error bars or seed information.

E6.justification: For the retained nominal 120-node low-noise setting, v1 Figure 5.1c reaches distance 8, whereas v2 Figure 5.1b is mostly zero with spikes at 2; the reason is unexplained. New high-noise curves report occasional distances around 42 and 400 and additional mean results. The stated Facebook1684 stability threshold of 0.04 conflicts with Figure 5.2b, which shows large discrepancies below that value.

T1.justification: Section 4 replaces the informal dense construction containing two cliques with a different random-graph family and Theorem 4.1. New derivations address expected degrees, Laplacian eigenvalues and convergence of the expected second-to-third eigenvalue ratio. v2 also adds Lemma 2.7 and the SBM connection in Remark 2.13. The main Theorem 3.1 and its assumptions remain substantially unchanged.

C1.justification: The central robustness claim for p = O(log n/n) and the claimed optimal privacy-budget order remain. However, the negative contribution changes from an explicitly dense counterexample to a non-sparse graph family, with the abstract dropping the dense qualification. v2 also explicitly claims that the earlier SBM result follows from its assumptions.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledges that the logarithmic privacy budget may be too large for applications, interprets large-noise behavior as graph-dependent, and explains that alternative partitions can still have low conductance. It adds average-case robustness interpretation and specific reasons why the proofs do not directly extend beyond two clusters.

D1.justification: v2 names Lanczos and a cited approximation approach as options for computing the eigenvector. It revises the second dataset filename and adds a general SNAP dataset reference. These are documentation changes; neither PDF establishes a changed implemented solver or supplies code, hardware or runtime information.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references concerning eigenvector approximation, network structure, SBM spectra and random-graph concentration, including Adil and Saranurak, Barabasi and Albert, Deng et al., and Lu and Peng. It removes the Ng et al. and Imola et al. 2022 references, clarifies dependence on Peng and Yoshida, and explicitly positions the theorem as covering prior SBM results.

P1.justification: The title, author information, acknowledgments and citation style change. Motivation, assumption explanations and concluding discussion are expanded, and the experiments gain two subsections. The six-section organization and much of the main proof prose remain, so the language and structural revision is limited.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a new publication layout and substantially reorganizes the visuals. It introduces the paired network illustration in Figure 1.1, redraws Figure 4.1 to show original and perturbed constructions, restructures Figure 5.1, and adds two-panel Figures 5.2 and 5.3.

improvement.justification: The added stress tests, mean summaries and practical qualifications provide useful evidence and context. However, the replacement instability argument contains an arithmetic inconsistency: Equation 4.2 reports 0.4 although its stated normalized eigenvector gives 0.1. Its formal conclusion concerns expected eigenvalues rather than directly quantifying clustering failure. Figure 5.2b also contradicts the stated 0.04 stability threshold. These problems affect important additions, preventing a reliable judgment that the benefits outweigh the weaknesses.
